senses.en: the floor; the ground (the surface you stand or walk on)
land; a plot of land (一块地)

measure.note: 一块地 'a plot of land'; 片 piàn for a wide stretch: 一片地

examples.en: Your floor is so clean!
examples.analysis: 地 here is the floor of a home. 你家的地 'your home's floor': owner + 的 + 地. 真 + adjective makes an exclamation, 'so clean!'. To say 'on the floor', Chinese adds 上: 地上 is its own word.

examples.en: Whose land is this?
examples.analysis: Here 地 means a piece of land, such as a field or a building plot. 这 + 块 + 地: 块 is the measure word for a plot, so 'this plot of land'. 是谁的 asks 'whose is it?', with the noun left out after 谁的.

examples.en: The floor isn't clean. Don't sit on it.
examples.analysis: 地 'the floor' is the subject, and 不干净 'is not clean' describes it: the adjective follows 不 directly, with no 是. 别坐 'don't sit (on it)' leaves the place out, because the listener can see where.

collocations.en: on the ground; on the floor

related.en: on the ground; on the floor (where something is)
a different word: the particle that links a describer to a verb (慢慢地走)

meaning: to enter; to go in; to come in

senses.en: to enter; to go in or come in (进 + place: 进商店)
the base of the direction verbs 进来 'come in' and 进去 'go in'

examples.en: Can we go in now?
examples.analysis: 进 'go in' has no place after it here: the place is clear from the situation. 能 + verb asks whether something is possible or allowed, and 吗 makes it a yes/no question. The subject is dropped because it is obvious.

examples.zh: 我们进商店吧，外边太热了。
examples.en: Let's go into the shop. It's too hot outside.
examples.analysis: 进 + place: 进商店 'go into the shop'. The place follows 进 directly, with no separate word for 'into'. 吧 turns the line into a suggestion, 'let's'. 太…了 = 'too…'.

examples.en: Don't go into my room!
examples.analysis: 别 + verb is a 'don't' command: 别进 'don't go in'. 我的房间 'my room' comes straight after 进 as its object. Bare 进 means moving in, but does not say whether the movement is toward or away from the speaker; 进来 'come in (toward me)' and 进去 'go in (away from me)' do.

collocations.en: to enter (through the door); to come or go in

related.en: to go in (away from the speaker)

senses.en: new (not used before; just bought or made)
new (recently arrived or begun: 新同学, 新年)

examples.en: There's a new student in our class.
examples.analysis: 新 goes straight before the noun: 新同学 'a new classmate', with no 的. 有个 is 有一个 with 一 dropped, which is common in casual speech. 我们班 'our class' also takes no 的.

examples.en: Is your phone new?
examples.analysis: 是 + 新的 'a new one' sorts the phone into a type: new, as opposed to old or second-hand. 新的 is 新 + 的 with the noun 手机 left out, since it has just been said. 吗 makes it a yes/no question.

examples.en: My car isn't new any more.
examples.analysis: 不 + adjective + 了 = 'no longer…': 了 marks a change, so 不新了 is 'not new any more'. Without 了, 我的车不新 would simply describe the car as not new.

related.en: old; long-standing (老朋友 'an old friend' vs 新朋友 'a new friend')

senses.en: you, said with respect: to older people, customers, patients, people you have just met

examples.en: Excuse me, are you Dr. Wang?
examples.analysis: 您 takes the same slot as 你, here the subject: 您 + 是 + 王医生. It shows respect to a stranger, an older person or a professional. 请问 'may I ask' opens a polite question, and surname + 医生 is a common way to address a doctor.

examples.en: Please have a seat. I'll go and get him.
examples.analysis: 您 at the front addresses the visitor respectfully: 您请坐 is the courteous form of 'please sit', as a receptionist or host would say it. In 去叫他, 叫 means 'to call someone over', not 'to be named'.

examples.en: No need to see me out. Goodbye!
examples.analysis: A guest says this to a host walking them to the door. 不用 + verb = 'there's no need to': 不用送 'no need to see me off'. 了 marks the change: you can stop here. 您 keeps it respectful.

related.en: you (more than one). 您 has no standard plural (您们 is avoided): a group is 你们, or politely 各位

senses.en: some; a few; a little (an amount you don't specify)
(after an adjective) a bit more: 慢一些 'a bit slower'

examples.en: I bought some fruit.
examples.analysis: 一些 goes before the noun, like English 'some': 一些水果 'some fruit'. It needs no measure word of its own (no 个), and it works both for things you count and things you don't.

examples.en: Take some of this bread.
examples.analysis: The bread is named first as the topic, 这些面包; then 一些 stands alone as the object of 拿, meaning 'some (of it)'. 吧 makes the offer friendly rather than an order.

examples.en: Could you speak a bit more slowly?
examples.analysis: After an adjective, 一些 means 'a bit more': 说慢一些 'speak a little slower'. 慢一点儿 means the same and is very common in speech. 好吗 at the end turns the request into a polite question.

related.en: a little; a bit (a small amount)
some (often opening a sentence: 有些人…)

senses.en: three; 3
third, before 楼, 月, 号 and similar: 三楼 'third floor', 三月 'March'

examples.en: There are three people in my family.
examples.analysis: Most nouns need a measure word between the number and the noun: 三 + 口 + 人. 口 is the measure for counting the members of a household, and 我家有… 'my family has…' is the usual way to give family size.

examples.en: Are the baozi three kuai each?
examples.analysis: Unit prices are often said as price + 一 + measure: 三块钱一个 'three kuai for one', so 'three each'. 块 is the spoken word for yuan. 吗 makes it a yes/no check before you buy.

examples.en: He hasn't come to work for three days.
examples.analysis: With 没, the length of time goes before the negative: 三天没来 'for three days hasn't come'. 天 needs no measure word, so 三天, not 三个天. The final 了 says the absence is still going on.

related.en: two (in counting and inside larger numbers: 十二); on its own before a measure word, usually 两 liǎng: 两个

senses.en: there; that place (away from the speaker)
after a person: that person's place: 小王那里 'at Xiao Wang's'

examples.en: Wait for me there.
examples.analysis: 在那里 'at that place' comes before the verb 等: with most verbs, the place where something happens goes before the verb, where English puts it after. 吧 softens the instruction into a suggestion.

examples.en: Is the food good there?
examples.analysis: 那里 + 的 describes the noun: 那里的菜 'the food there', literally 'that place's dishes'. The place word comes first, linked by 的, where English puts 'there' at the end.

examples.en: I've never been there.
examples.analysis: 那里 is the object of 去过 'have been to'. 没 + verb + 过 = 'have never done'. 那儿 means the same; it is more typical of northern, Beijing-style speech, while 那里 is used everywhere and in writing.

related.en: where? (哪 has the third tone, 那 the fourth)

senses.en: happy; glad; in a good mood
glad to (高兴 + verb): 很高兴认识你 'glad to meet you'

examples.en: Nice to meet you.
examples.analysis: The set phrase on meeting someone, literally 'knowing you, (I) am glad'. 认识你 is the topic and 很高兴 the comment. 很 is the usual link before an adjective here and is said lightly, so it adds little 'very'. 很高兴认识你 says the same and is at least as common.

examples.en: I'm so glad you could come.
examples.analysis: The first clause gives the cause, the second the feeling: 你能来 'that you could come', then 我真高兴 'I'm really glad'. 真 + adjective is warmer and stronger than 很. Chinese often puts the cause first; English puts it after.

examples.en: What's made you upset?
examples.analysis: 不高兴 'not happy' usually means upset or annoyed, not just neutral. 怎么 before the verb phrase asks 'how come?', with a note of surprise. 了 marks a change: the person seemed fine before.

collocations.en: glad; pleased (in set phrases like 很高兴认识你, 很 adds little 'very')

related.en: happy; joyful (in wishes: 生日快乐 'happy birthday')

senses.en: old; elderly (of people and animals)
old; long-standing; from the past: 老同学, 老房子

examples.en: My grandma is getting old. She walks slowly.
examples.analysis: 老 + 了 = 'has grown old': 了 marks the change, so 老了 is about getting old, not a fixed label. With 了 the adjective can stand alone, without 很. 走路很慢 'walks slowly' adds what that looks like.

examples.en: He's an old classmate of mine.
examples.analysis: Before 同学, 老 means 'of long standing', not 'elderly': a 老同学 is someone you were at school with years ago, whatever their age. (In 老人 'old person', 老 does mean elderly.) 老 goes straight before the noun with no 的.

examples.en: You're not old at all!
examples.analysis: 一点儿也不 + adjective = 'not … at all'. 老 here is about a person's age. It is a friendly reply when someone sighs 我老了 'I'm getting old'.

related.en: new (老朋友 'old friend' vs 新朋友 'new friend')

senses.en: first; before something else (先…再… 'first…, then…')
before other people: 我先走了 'I'll be off now'
for now; for the time being (先别… 'don't… yet')

examples.en: I'll be off now.
examples.analysis: The everyday way to excuse yourself: 先 'before the rest of you' + 走 'leave'. 了 signals the change that is about to happen. 先 sits before the verb, where English would say 'I'll go first'.

examples.en: Have a cup of tea before you go.
examples.analysis: 先 + first action, 再 + second action = 'first…, then…'. 喝杯茶 is 喝一杯茶 with 一 dropped, as is common in speech. 吧 makes it a warm invitation, the kind a host offers a guest who wants to leave.

examples.en: Don't tell him yet.
examples.analysis: 先 + 别 = 'don't… for now': 先 here means 'for the time being', so the message is 'not yet', not 'never'. Compare plain 别告诉他 'don't tell him', which sets no time limit.

senses.en: to buy; to purchase

examples.en: Have you bought your plane ticket?
examples.analysis: 买 + object + 了吗 asks whether something has been done: 'have you bought…?'. A short answer is 买了 'yes, I have' or 还没买 'not yet'; 不买 would mean 'I won't buy it'.

examples.en: Where did you buy it?
examples.analysis: This asks about a purchase that already happened. The (是)…的 frame puts the focus on where: 在哪儿 + 买 + 的. 是 is dropped, as it often is in speech, and the thing bought is left out because both sides know it.

examples.en: It's too expensive. I won't buy it after all.
examples.analysis: 不 + 买 + 了 = 'I won't buy it after all': the final 了 marks a change of plan. 没买 would instead report that you didn't buy it. 太…了 'too…' gives the reason first.

collocations.en: to pay the bill (in a restaurant)

related.en: to sell (fourth tone; 买 has the third)

senses.en: doctor; physician
as a title after a surname: 王医生 'Dr. Wang'

measure.note: 一个医生; 位 wèi is the polite measure: 一位医生

examples.en: I'm a doctor. I work at a hospital.
examples.analysis: 是 + 医生 states your job; Chinese needs no word for 'a'. The second clause drops the repeated 我, and 在医院 'at a hospital' comes before the verb 工作, place before action.

examples.en: Is there a doctor here?
examples.analysis: Place + 有 + noun = 'there is … (in that place)': 这里有医生 'there's a doctor here', and 吗 turns it into a question. This is a line you might call out in an emergency (有没有医生？ is also said).

examples.zh: 医生今天不上班，明天再来吧。
examples.en: The doctor isn't working today. Come back tomorrow.
examples.analysis: 医生 is the subject, and the context makes it 'the doctor', a specific one; Chinese has no word for 'the'. 不上班 'isn't at work'. 再来吧 'come again' is a gentle instruction, as a receptionist would give it.

related.en: to see a doctor; (of a doctor) to see patients

senses.en: last; final (before a noun: 最后一天 'the last day')
in the end; finally (before the verb, or opening a clause)

examples.en: Who's having the last baozi?
examples.analysis: 最后 + 一 + 个 + noun = 'the last …': 最后 comes before the number and the measure word. The phrase opens the sentence as the topic, then 谁吃 'who eats (it)?' asks about it.

examples.en: In the end we went by train.
examples.analysis: Here 最后 means 'in the end', after other options. It goes after the subject and before the verb phrase. 坐火车去的 uses the (是)…的 frame to say how a past trip was made.

examples.zh: 我等了他一个小时，最后他也没来。
examples.en: I waited an hour for him, and in the end he still didn't come.
examples.analysis: 最后 opens the second clause: 'in the end', after the hour of waiting. After effort that comes to nothing, 也 (or 还是) adds 'even so': 最后他也没来 'in the end he still didn't come'. Plain 最后他没来 is also fine. 最后 can also follow the subject: 他最后也没来.

related.en: afterwards; later (in a story about the past)

senses.en: hand

measure.note: 一只手 'one hand'; 双 shuāng for a pair: 一双手

examples.en: My hands are cold.
examples.analysis: Body parts often take the owner with no 的: 我手 'my hand(s)'; 我的手 is also fine. 手 has no plural form, so 'hand' or 'hands' comes from context. 很 links the adjective 冷 to the subject.

examples.en: Put your hand here. Don't move.
examples.analysis: A clinic-style instruction. 手 comes first as the topic, then 放这儿 'put (it) here'; 'your' is left out because it is obvious. 别动 'don't move' follows as a second instruction.

examples.en: Can I eat it with my hands?
examples.analysis: 用 + 手 + verb = 'use your hands to…': 用手吃 'eat with your hands'. The 用 phrase comes before the main verb, where English puts 'with…' after it. 能…吗 asks whether it is OK.

senses.en: where? (asks about a place)
with 都, or with 也 + a negative: anywhere (哪儿也不去 'not going anywhere'; 哪儿都行 'anywhere is fine')

examples.en: Where's the restroom?
examples.analysis: Thing + 在 + 哪儿 = 'where is…?'. 哪儿 sits where the answer will go: the reply is 洗手间在那儿 'it's over there'. No 吗 is added, because 哪儿 already makes it a question.

examples.en: I don't know where he is.
examples.analysis: 他在哪儿 'where he is' is the object of 知道, with the same word order as the question 他在哪儿？; English switches 'where is he' to 'where he is'. The whole sentence is a statement, not a question.

examples.en: I'm not going anywhere today.
examples.analysis: 哪儿 + 也 + negative = 'not … anywhere': here 哪儿 is not a question. It comes before the verb, so 哪儿也不去 is literally 'anywhere also not go'. 哪儿都不去 means the same.

related.en: where? (also common, especially in the south and in writing)
there (那 has the fourth tone; 哪 the third)

senses.en: woman (an adult female; the general word, paired with 男人)

measure.note: 一个女人; politely 一位女士 'a lady'

examples.zh: 这工作，男人女人都能做。
examples.en: Both men and women can do this job.
examples.analysis: 男人女人 'men and women' is a pair with no word for 'and', common for natural pairs. 都 'all, both' comes after the people it covers and before the verb. 这工作 'this job' opens the sentence as the topic.

examples.en: There's a woman at the door looking for you.
examples.analysis: 有个 + person + verb introduces someone new: 'there's a woman … looking for you'. 女人 is the plain word here; many speakers would say 女的, which is more casual, or 女士 to be polite.

examples.zh: 你们医院女人比男人多吗？
examples.en: Are there more women than men at your hospital?
examples.analysis: A 比 comparison: 女人 + 比 + 男人 + 多 'women, compared with men, are many', so 'more women than men'. 你们医院 'your hospital' is the topic up front, and 吗 makes it a yes/no question.

related.en: lady; Ms. (polite, for a woman you don't know well)

senses.en: name (of a person; also of a shop, a dish, a place)

examples.en: What's your name?
examples.analysis: 叫 + 什么名字 = 'be called what name?': 名字 is the object of 叫. The answer puts the name in that slot: 我叫王明. To an adult in a formal setting, 您贵姓 (asking the surname) is more polite.

examples.en: Please write your name here.
examples.analysis: 名字 is the object of 写 'write'. 你的名字 'your name' uses 的; 你名字 also occurs in casual talk. 在这儿 'here' goes before the verb, and 请 at the front makes it a polite request.

examples.en: I've forgotten his name.
examples.analysis: 名字 is the object of 忘了 'forgot'. 了 follows the verb to show that the forgetting has happened. 他的名字 'his name': owner + 的 + 名字.

collocations.en: to choose a name (for a baby, a pet)

meaning: to know (a person); to get to know; to recognize

senses.en: to know; to be acquainted with (a person, a place)
to get to know; to meet for the first time (我们是…认识的)
to recognize; to be able to read (a character)

examples.en: Do you know each other?
examples.analysis: 认识 has no object here: with a plural subject, 你们认识 means 'you know each other'. It is about being acquainted with a person; for knowing a fact, Chinese uses 知道.

examples.en: We met in Beijing.
examples.analysis: Here 认识 means 'got to know each other', the start of the acquaintance; English says 'met'. 是…的 puts the focus on where it happened: 是 + 在北京 + 认识 + 的.

examples.en: I can't read any of these characters.
examples.analysis: With characters, 认识 means 'recognize, can read'. The object 这些字 moves to the front as the topic so that 都 can cover it: 都不认识 'don't know any of them'. 不都认识 would mean 'don't know every one of them' (some, but not all).

collocations.en: not to know (someone); not to recognize
to be able to read characters

related.en: to know (a fact or a piece of information)

meaning: to sit; to travel by (bus, train, plane)

senses.en: to sit; to take a seat
to travel by; to ride as a passenger: 坐火车, 坐飞机

examples.en: Why don't you sit here?
examples.analysis: The place can follow 坐 directly: 坐这儿 'sit here'. 坐在这儿 and 在这儿坐 also work. 吧 makes it an offer rather than an order.

examples.en: Are you going by plane?
examples.analysis: 坐 + vehicle + 去 = 'go by…': the means of travel comes before the main verb 去. 坐 is for vehicles you ride as a passenger; driving yourself is 开车.

examples.en: Don't sit there. That's Lao Li's seat.
examples.analysis: 别 + 坐 = 'don't sit'. 那儿 'there' follows 坐 directly, as in the first example. 那是老李的 'that's Lao Li's' leaves out the noun 'seat', which is clear from the situation.

collocations.en: to go by car or bus

senses.en: to drink (water, tea, milk; also soup)

examples.en: What would you like to drink?
examples.analysis: 想 + 喝 = 'want to drink'. 什么 'what' stays in the object slot after 喝, exactly where the answer goes: 我想喝茶. Chinese does not move the question word to the front as English does.

examples.en: I don't drink tea in the evening.
examples.analysis: 不 + 喝 states a habit: 'I don't drink (tea)'. The time word 晚上 'in the evening' goes before 不喝; English puts it at the end.

examples.en: Is this water OK to drink?
examples.analysis: 这水 'this water' comes first as the topic, then 能喝吗 'can (it) be drunk?'; Chinese needs no passive here. 这 and 那 can stand straight before a noun like 水 with no measure word (这个水 is also said).
